first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), and the inherited record most directly aimed at that is memory_86 (shortening onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value), reinforced by memory_31 (signup simplification lifted SMB activation) and memory_91 (in-product activation messaging). Onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a completion/time-to-value fix plausibly recovers both metrics, which is why I picked it over activation_messaging for the single slot. I want memory_86 verified because I am leaning the whole week on it and I only have the consolidated summary, not the original design, sample, or durability window; if the source record shows a short measurement horizon or a self-serve-only cohort that no longer resembles today's mix, I would downshift to a small_guarded_test or swap to activation_messaging. I want memory_73 verified because the competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the obvious reflex, and that memory carries an explicit defect on its face: the readout pooled two cohorts after a mid-test redefinition, so its 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' may be an artifact of the pooling rather than a real effect. Before I decline the pricing response in a quarter where we are actively losing price-sensitive SMB accounts, I should know whether that evidence survives inspection. Referral incentive (memory_57) targets established customers and does not address the funnel decay; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment from where the bleeding is. Downstream value risk: promotional pricing would likely buy discount-anchored accounts with weaker retention, which is acquisition volume rather than sustainable qualified revenue; and even simplified onboarding can trade signup volume for lead quality, so I will instrument this on qualified-account and week-four retention outcomes, not raw completion, and treat the inherited lifts as directional priors rather than established results.
